design_detail: Single-author retrospective case series from the files of one forensic pathology department (Medico-Legal Centre, Sheffield, UK): 77 medico-legal autopsies, 1992–2008, in which MDMA, MDEA or MBDB was detected on post-mortem toxicology. Every death had a full autopsy with histology; femoral blood, urine and stomach contents were analysed in one hospital laboratory (GC–MS with selected ion monitoring). Deaths were grouped by the cause of death given (MDMA or related-drug toxicity, polydrug use, trauma), and blood MDMA was described for each group by range, mean and median (Table 1), without statistical tests or individual values. The Discussion compares the results with published series from New York, a US medical-examiner survey, Melbourne, Sydney and Taiwan, and with one study of paired ante-mortem and post-mortem samples. Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist because it describes the distribution of a measurement in defined groups of deaths; there is no living comparison group.
can_establish: The range, mean and median of femoral blood MDMA concentrations at autopsy in one English centre's deaths attributed to MDMA toxicity, to polydrug use and to trauma between 1992 and 2008, and that the three ranges overlap widely.
cannot_establish: A fatal or toxic MDMA threshold, the concentrations found in living people after ordinary use (trauma deaths are an assumed, not a measured, non-fatal baseline), how far post-mortem redistribution or survival time shifted any value, or whether the cause-of-death groups were assigned independently of the measured concentrations.

sample.recruitment: Records: deaths in which ring-substituted phenethylamines were detected on post-mortem toxicology, identified from the files of the Department of Forensic Pathology at the Medico-Legal Centre, Sheffield, UK, for 1992–2008 (p. 249, Materials and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). How the files were searched, and how many autopsies were tested for these drugs, is not described.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Inclusion: positive post-mortem toxicology for MDMA, MDEA or MBDB. No exclusions stated. Table 1 includes only deaths with MDMA measured in blood (59 of 77); deaths with MDMA in urine only, with only liver available (one decomposed body) or with MDEA or MBDB alone are outside it (pp. 248–249).
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex or other characteristics are given for the series or for any group. Place of collapse: for the MDMA-toxicity deaths, most often at home and next most often at a nightclub; for the polydrug deaths, 27 of 30 at home and 3 at a nightclub (p. 249, Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 18 of the 77 deaths have no value in Table 1 (editors' count from p. 249): 4 of the 17 MDMA-toxicity deaths (apparently the water-intoxication, myocardial-necrosis, delayed-hyperpyrexia and decomposed cases, which the paper does not say outright), 8 of the 30 polydrug deaths, 4 of the 28 traumatic deaths (MDMA found in urine only) and the two deaths outside the three groups.
sample.selection_effects: Only deaths that reached a medico-legal autopsy with toxicology in one English centre, and in which an amphetamine derivative was found, are included; the series cannot show how many MDMA-related deaths were missed elsewhere. The trauma group is not a sample of people who use MDMA without harm: it is people who died by homicide, vehicle collision, fall or drowning with MDMA present, in some of whom MDMA may have contributed to the event, and whose time since use is unknown. The cause-of-death groups were assigned by unnamed certifiers on unstated criteria, presumably with the concentrations known, which would tend to place high values in the MDMA-toxicity group.

exposure.measurement: MDMA concentration (mg/l) in femoral blood taken at full autopsy; urine and stomach contents also analysed; GC–MS with selected ion monitoring after butyl acetate extraction and acetylation, by the Department of Clinical Chemistry, Royal Hallamshire Hospital, Sheffield (p. 249, Materials and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). No validation data, limits of detection or method changes over the 16 years are reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: no data on amounts, timing, route or pattern of use. The Discussion notes that the number of tablets taken and what tablets sold as MDMA contain both vary (p. 250).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drugs are counted, without concentrations, for the polydrug group (cannabinoids 16, ethanol 13, heroin 11, benzodiazepines 9, amphetamine 8, antidepressants 6, methadone 5, cocaine 5, GHB 2) and the trauma group (ethanol 17, cannabinoids 10, amphetamine 5, cocaine 4, antidepressants 2, ketamine 1) (p. 249). They are not reported for the MDMA-toxicity group, which the abstract describes as deaths from MDMA alone. MDA, the metabolite, is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (post-mortem samples). The time from use to death and from death to sampling is not reported for any death; one MDMA-toxicity death was a delayed death from hyperpyrexia.

comparison.controls: No living comparison group. The comparison is between cause-of-death groups: the 24 traumatic deaths with MDMA in blood (from homicide, vehicle collision, fall from height and drowning) are treated by the author as a baseline for non-fatal concentrations (p. 250, Discussion, 5th paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance, pattern of use, time of last use, survival interval, interval from death to autopsy, condition of the body and natural disease are not reported for any group.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Trauma group: ethanol in 17, cannabinoids in 10, amphetamine in 5, cocaine in 4, antidepressants in 2 and ketamine in 1 of the 28 deaths (p. 249, Results, 4th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Femoral blood MDMA concentration at autopsy; cause of death as given (MDMA or related-drug toxicity, polydrug use, trauma), with the mechanism named for the atypical MDMA-toxicity deaths (water intoxication, myocardial necrosis, delayed hyperpyrexia).
outcomes.validity_norms: No criteria are given for attributing a death to MDMA toxicity rather than to polydrug use, and who attributed it (pathologist, coroner) is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: MDMA death: MDMA (or related-drug) toxicity given as the cause of death. Polydrug death: polydrug use given as the cause. Trauma: a traumatic death. Fatal against non-fatal concentration is operationalized as MDMA-toxicity deaths against traumatic deaths with MDMA present.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; whoever gave the cause of death is likely to have known the concentrations (editors' inference; the paper does not say).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only (Table 1, p. 250): MDMA toxicity (N=13) range 0.478–53.9 mg/l, mean 8.43, median 3.49; polydrug (N=22) 0.04–41.5 mg/l, mean 2.90 (2.78 in the Results text), median 0.76; trauma (N=24) 0.035–4.81 mg/l, mean 0.862, median 0.483. No test, interval or individual values. Editors' calculation: the MDMA-toxicity median is about 7.2 times the trauma median and 4.6 times the polydrug median; from the printed medians and ranges, at least 7 of the 13 MDMA-toxicity values lie inside the trauma range and at least 12 of the 24 trauma values lie inside the MDMA-toxicity range. The MDMA-toxicity mean is more than twice its median, so a few very high values dominate it.
analysis.selective_reporting: Individual concentrations, other drugs found in the MDMA-toxicity group, MDA concentrations and the values for the 18 deaths outside Table 1 are not reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive); groups of 13, 22 and 24 values.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 77 Sheffield deaths with an amphetamine derivative detected, 17 were attributed principally to MDMA, 30 to polydrug use and 28 to trauma. Femoral blood MDMA ranged 0.478–53.9 mg/l (median 3.49) in the 13 MDMA-toxicity deaths with a blood value, 0.04–41.5 mg/l (median 0.76) in 22 polydrug deaths and 0.035–4.81 mg/l (median 0.483) in 24 traumatic deaths. The ranges overlap widely, while the medians differ about sevenfold between MDMA-toxicity and traumatic deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state that no specific concentration can determine death without the history and full autopsy findings, and that there is no specific toxic or fatal MDMA concentration (pp. 248, 251); the key points say fatal MDMA concentrations overlap with non-fatal ones (p. 251). The overlap is supported, and a classification made with the concentrations known would, if anything, have exaggerated the separation, so the conclusion is conservative in that respect. The step from trauma deaths to non-fatal or tolerated concentrations is an assumption: the Discussion says trauma concentrations are “likely to equate with those of normal recreational use” (p. 250), but no living people were studied, the timing of use is unknown, and MDMA may have contributed to some falls, drownings and collisions. The abstract gives the numbers with blood values (13, 22, 24) as if they were the group sizes (17, 30, 28) and calls the MDMA-toxicity deaths deaths from MDMA alone, which the results do not document.

timeline.event: Early UK report of toxicity and deaths after ecstasy, cited by Milroy among reports of collapse at raves and nightclubs (ref. 26).

Gill et al., New York 1997–2002: 22 deaths with MDMA; MDMA and its metabolites the only drugs in just two autopsied cases; mean blood MDMA 1.04 mg/l in acute MDMA intoxication deaths and 0.97 mg/l in trauma deaths (as summarized by Milroy, p. 249).

Patel et al.: survey of US medical examiner offices (8% response), 102 deaths with MDMA; heart blood used in 66%; mean MDMA 2.02 mg/l in heart and 1.12 mg/l in femoral blood, difference not significant (as summarized, p. 250).

Elliott: MDMA in ante-mortem and post-mortem samples from deaths after hospital admission; one case with heart blood 28.39 mg/l against femoral 6.19 and 7.25 mg/l two days after death (as summarized, p. 250). Also listed by Borra et al. (2026) among ante-mortem/post-mortem comparison studies.
Ferner's review of post-mortem clinical pharmacology records published lethal MDMA ranges spanning 40–8500 µg/L (as recorded on its study card).

Pilgrim et al. (Melbourne), Kaye et al. (Sydney) and Lin et al. (Taiwan, 59 deaths, ketamine in 28): wide, overlapping MDMA ranges across cause-of-death groups; in Melbourne the trauma median (1.03 mg/l) exceeded the drug-overdose median (0.05 mg/l) (as summarized, p. 250).
Review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research lists MDMA and MDA among drugs found higher in femoral blood after death than in samples taken before death.

replication.where_it_stands: Overlap of blood MDMA between deaths attributed to MDMA and other deaths with MDMA present is consistent across the series Milroy summarizes (New York, Melbourne, Sydney, Taiwan), all small and retrospective; in the editors' reading the causes of death were probably given with the concentrations known, but neither this paper nor its summaries say so. Henry et al. (1992), read in this round, give plasma MDMA in 8 people who survived after severe complications or road accidents (0.05–0.97 mg/l) that overlaps the levels in their deaths (0.11–1.26 mg/l); no study read here compares post-mortem femoral blood MDMA with levels in living people after ordinary use. Redistribution reviews (Borra et al., 2026) report MDMA among drugs whose femoral concentrations after death exceed those measured before death.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement in the article. The acknowledgment thanks a member of the Royal Hallamshire Hospital clinical chemistry department for information on analytical techniques (p. 251).
funding.affiliations_note: The author is at the Eastern Ontario Forensic Pathology Unit (Ontario Forensic Pathology Service, The Ottawa Hospital) and the University of Ottawa; the cases come from the Sheffield Medico-Legal Centre files. Whether the author performed or certified any of these autopsies is not stated. Several cited papers are his own (refs. 17, 22, 30).

what_would_settle_it: A multi-centre post-mortem series reporting individual femoral blood MDMA values with the interval from use to death and from death to sampling, with causes of death assigned by pathologists who did not see the concentrations or by prespecified criteria, set against MDMA concentrations measured in living people (emergency department or roadside samples) and in deaths from causes clearly unrelated to MDMA with known timing.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to address the target population
domains.note: One centre's medico-legal autopsies with an amphetamine derivative detected, 1992–2008: suits the question for that centre, not for MDMA deaths generally; the share of all autopsies tested is not given.

domains.domain: 2. Study participants sampled in an appropriate way
domains.note: Apparently every positive case in the department's files, but how the files were searched and whether the list is complete is not described.
13, 22 and 24 blood values; a single value (53.9 mg/l) can move a group mean by several mg/l.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: No age, sex, circumstances, survival time, hospital treatment or interval from death to autopsy for any group.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 18 of 77 deaths are outside Table 1, including the four atypical MDMA-toxicity deaths; reasons are given only in part.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used for identification of the condition
domains.note: The cause-of-death category was given by unnamed certifiers on unstated criteria, presumably with the concentrations known; the trauma group is defined by mechanism of death, not by absence of an MDMA effect.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: Femoral blood at full autopsy and one laboratory and method for all, but no validation data, no account of method changes over 16 years, and no interval from death to sampling.
Ranges and medians are appropriate for skewed values, but there are no individual values, intervals or tests, and the polydrug mean is printed two ways.

domains.domain: 9. Response rate adequate, or low response managed appropriately

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI prevalence checklist for a descriptive case series. Editors' summary: high risk of bias, because the groups are small, unstated certifiers assigned the causes of death on unstated criteria and probably with the concentrations known, the trauma group is an assumed rather than a measured non-fatal comparison, and the timing of use and of sampling is unknown. The main bias would increase the apparent separation between MDMA-toxicity and trauma deaths, so the paper's central point (wide overlap, no fatal threshold) is the safer use. Citable for: the ranges and medians in Table 1 with their group sizes; the overlap between groups; the share of deaths with an amphetamine derivative present that were attributed to MDMA (17 of 77); the drugs found alongside MDMA in polydrug and trauma deaths. Not citable for: a fatal or toxic concentration; trauma-death concentrations as the levels of ordinary recreational use; the polydrug mean without noting the two printed values.

key_findings.finding: How deaths entered the series and were grouped: deaths with ring-substituted phenethylamines detected on post-mortem toxicology, from the files of the Department of Forensic Pathology, Medico-Legal Centre, Sheffield, 1992–2008; each had a full autopsy with histology, and femoral blood, urine and stomach contents went to the Royal Hallamshire Hospital clinical chemistry department for GC–MS. Deaths were divided by the cause of death given: MDMA or related-drug toxicity, polydrug use, or trauma. Who gave the cause and on what criteria is not stated.

Seventy-seven deaths had positive toxicology: MDMA in 73, MDEA in 4 (2 of them with MDMA) and MBDB in 2. 17 deaths were attributed principally to MDMA, 30 to polydrug use and 28 to trauma, with one hypothermia death (traces of MDMA and amphetamine in urine) and one attributed mainly to ischaemic heart disease (several drugs at relatively low concentrations, MDMA among them). Editors' calculation: 22% of the deaths with an amphetamine derivative present were attributed principally to MDMA, 39% to polydrug use and 36% to trauma.

Of the 17 deaths attributed to MDMA, one was from water intoxication, one from myocardial necrosis, one a delayed death from hyperpyrexia, and one body was decomposed with only liver available; in the other 13 death was known or presumed to have been rapid. Collapse was most often at home, next most often at a nightclub.

Polydrug deaths: in 28 of 30 MDMA was the main drug (one each MDEA and MBDB); MDMA was in blood in 22 (0.04–41.5 mg/l, median 0.76). Other principal drugs: cannabinoids 16, ethanol 13, heroin 11, benzodiazepines 9, amphetamine 8, antidepressants 6, methadone 5, cocaine 5, GHB 2. Collapse was at home in 27 and at a nightclub in 3, the three each involving amphetamine with MDMA, MDEA or MBDB.
key_findings.note: The polydrug mean is 2.78 mg/l in this paragraph and 2.90 mg/l in Table 1 and the abstract (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Traumatic deaths: 28 (homicide 8, vehicle collision 10, fall from height 6, drowning 4); MDMA in blood in 24 (0.035–4.81 mg/l, mean 0.862, median 0.483) and in urine only in the rest; other drugs found: ethanol 17, cannabinoids 10, amphetamine 5, cocaine 4, antidepressants 2, ketamine 1.

Blood MDMA at autopsy (Table 1): MDMA-toxicity deaths (N=13) 0.478–53.9 mg/l, mean 8.43, median 3.49; mixed-drug deaths (N=22) 0.04–41.5 mg/l, mean 2.90, median 0.76; trauma deaths (N=24) 0.035–4.81 mg/l, mean 0.862, median 0.483. No individual values or tests are given.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed medians and ranges: at least 7 of the 13 MDMA-toxicity values lie within the trauma range and at least 12 of the 24 trauma values lie within the MDMA-toxicity range; the MDMA-toxicity median is about 7.2 times the trauma median.

key_findings.finding: The author concludes that there is no specific toxic or fatal MDMA concentration, that a post-mortem concentration cannot give the cause of death without the history and the other autopsy findings, and that concentrations were nonetheless higher in MDMA-toxicity deaths than in polydrug and trauma deaths; he likens MDMA to cocaine and methamphetamine in the overlap between tolerated concentrations and concentrations seen at death.

The author treats trauma deaths as a baseline for non-fatal concentrations and as likely to reflect ordinary recreational use, and names two main problems in reading fatal cases: whether post-mortem concentrations reflect those before death, and post-mortem redistribution of MDMA (high volume of distribution), with heart blood showing the highest concentrations.

Paired samples cited from Elliott (second-hand): in 5 deaths after hospital admission, ante-mortem MDMA was 0.55–4.33 mg/l and post-mortem values ran from 0.47 to 28.39 mg/l; in one case, post-mortem samples taken 2 days after death gave heart blood 28.39 mg/l, right femoral 6.19, left femoral 7.25 and vitreous 11.93 mg/l, against ante-mortem serum of 4.33 mg/l taken a day before death.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: in that case heart blood was about 3.9–4.6 times femoral blood, and femoral blood about 1.4–1.7 times the serum value from the day before death. Serum and whole blood differ, so this ratio is indicative only.

key_findings.finding: Other series as summarized (second-hand): Patel et al., 102 deaths from 38 US medical examiner offices (8% of offices responded), heart blood in 66% of cases, mean MDMA 2.02 mg/l (SD 2.84) in heart and 1.12 mg/l (SD 1.23) in femoral blood, not significantly different; Melbourne, drug overdose median 0.05 mg/l and trauma median 1.03 mg/l; Sydney, MDMA-only deaths median 0.7 mg/l (0.3–64.0) and combined-toxicity deaths 0.9 mg/l (0.03–93.0); Taiwan (Lin et al.), 59 deaths, ketamine in 28, MDMA-only deaths median 2.77 mg/l and trauma deaths with ketamine median 0.97 mg/l.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; the Melbourne heart-disease median (0.3 mg/l) lies below its own printed range (0.5–2.6 mg/l), see reporting issues. Cite the primary series.

key_findings.finding: The author notes that MDMA is most often taken with alcohol and other drugs and that mono-intoxication is less common, that deciding which of the drugs present were relevant to death is difficult and has no easy answer (with methadone's effect on the QTc interval as an example), that water-intoxication deaths may show low MDMA because of haemodilution, and that most deaths in this series occurred at home rather than at raves.

reporting_issues.issue: The polydrug group's mean blood MDMA is 2.78 mg/l in the Results text (p. 249) but 2.90 mg/l in Table 1 (p. 250) and the abstract (p. 248); range and median agree.
reporting_issues.consequence: One mean is misprinted; cite the median (0.76 mg/l) and range, or both printed means.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 13 MDMA-toxicity, 22 polydrug and 24 trauma deaths; these are the deaths with MDMA measured in blood. The Results give 17, 30 and 28 deaths in these categories (p. 249).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract understates the group sizes; cite the category totals and the blood-value subsets separately.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract attributes the 13 deaths to the toxic effects of MDMA alone, but the paper lists other drugs only for the polydrug and trauma groups and reports nothing on other drugs in the MDMA-toxicity group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the MDMA-toxicity deaths were single-drug deaths cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Who assigned the cause of death (pathologist, coroner), on what criteria, and whether the measured concentration entered that decision is not stated, although the three groups are defined by it (Materials and methods, 3rd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible incorporation bias: if high concentrations led to an MDMA-toxicity verdict, the groups' difference in medians is partly built in. The overlap finding is not weakened by this.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals from use to death and from death to sampling are not reported for any case, although the Discussion names the gap between post-mortem and ante-mortem concentrations and post-mortem redistribution as the main problems of interpretation (p. 250).
reporting_issues.consequence: How far redistribution or survival time shifted the values in each group cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: In the summary of the Melbourne series, 5 deaths associated with heart disease are given a range of 0.5–2.6 mg/l and a median of 0.3 mg/l, a median below the minimum. In the Elliott summary, post-mortem values are printed as 0.47 and 28.39 mg/l, apparently a range.
reporting_issues.consequence: Second-hand figures with a printing error; take them from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes 77 deaths in which MDMA was detected; the Results say MDMA was found in 73, the other 4 having MDEA or MBDB without MDMA (p. 249).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the series is of deaths with any of three amphetamine derivatives.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Forensic Sci Med Pathol 7:248–252, pp. 248–252 (all pages; Table 1 and every number on this card checked on rendered pages; no supplement; no funding or conflict statement in the article).
verification.checked_by: AI reader 331 (blind second reading) and AI reader 350 (adjudication)

disagreements.first_pass: Overlap of blood MDMA between deaths attributed to MDMA and other deaths with MDMA present is consistent across the series Milroy summarizes (New York, Melbourne, Sydney, Taiwan), all small, retrospective and classified by certifiers who knew the concentrations. No study read here compares post-mortem MDMA concentrations with those of living people who use MDMA. Redistribution reviews (Borra et al., 2026) report MDMA among drugs whose femoral concentrations after death exceed those measured before death.
disagreements.reviewer: Editor's lead for this round (adjudication brief, Milroy): that certifiers knew the levels is an editors' inference; neither Milroy nor Darke says whether certifiers knew them. Second reader 331 made the same point on the claims; the Henry survivors were raised by 331 on the Henry card.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking p. 249 (Materials and methods, 3rd paragraph: deaths divided by the cause of death 'given'; no certifier, criteria or knowledge of levels stated) and pp. 249–250 for the summarized series. The unhedged clause is reworded as the editors' inference, and the sentence on living people now names Henry et al. (1992) Tables II–III (rendered pp. 385–386), so it no longer says that no study read here gives levels in living people.

disagreements.first_pass: Not reported; whoever gave the cause of death is likely to have known the concentrations.
disagreements.reviewer: Same lead (inference about certifiers' knowledge of the levels).
disagreements.resolution: Labelled as the editors' inference (p. 249, Materials and methods, 3rd paragraph). Judgment unchanged.
